body:
How petroleum reaches consumers

Crude oil may travel from an oilfield to a refinery through a crude-oil pipeline or by tanker. Imported crude is commonly unloaded at a coastal terminal before entering storage facilities or pipelines. After refining, petrol, diesel, aviation fuel and other products move to depots and markets through product pipelines, rail tank wagons, road tankers and coastal shipping.

Crude-oil pipelines and petroleum-product pipelines serve different stages of the supply chain. An oil tanker carries bulk liquid petroleum by sea; a refinery converts crude into products; and distribution depots supply retailers and industrial consumers.

Why international oil prices change

International crude-oil prices respond to global demand, available production, inventories, geopolitical developments and expectations about future supply. Brent and Dubai/Oman are important reference prices for different traded crude streams and regional markets.

Crude oils differ in density and sulphur content. Light crude is relatively less dense than heavy crude. Sweet crude has relatively low sulphur content, while sour crude contains more sulphur. These characteristics influence refining requirements and commercial prices.

India imports crude from multiple countries. Its import bill is affected not only by the quantity imported but also by the dollar price of crude, freight, insurance and the rupee-dollar exchange rate.

OPEC and international supply

OPEC stands for the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. It is an intergovernmental organisation of petroleum-exporting states that coordinates petroleum policies among its members. OPEC+ refers to cooperation between OPEC members and certain other oil-producing countries.

Production decisions by major exporters can influence international oil supply and prices. They are not the only determinant: demand changes, non-member production, inventories and international events also matter.

Why maritime routes are strategically important

Crude petroleum and LNG often move through international sea routes. Disruptions at important passages such as the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait or routes connected with the Suez Canal can increase journey times, insurance costs or supply risks.

A disruption does not necessarily stop every shipment. Suppliers and shipping companies may use alternative routes, but these can be longer or more expensive. Diversifying suppliers and maintaining adequate stocks can reduce exposure to some disruptions.

Retail petroleum prices

The retail price of petrol or diesel should not be equated directly with the price of one barrel of crude oil. Costs and charges can include crude procurement, refining and distribution, dealer margins and applicable taxes. Changes in tax rates or exchange rates can affect domestic prices independently of short-term movements in international crude benchmarks.

Price formation can differ among crude oil, petrol, diesel, LPG and natural gas. A single international oil price therefore does not determine all Indian energy prices through one uniform formula.

Strategic petroleum reserves

A strategic petroleum reserve (SPR) is crude-oil storage maintained to help respond to serious supply disruptions and other emergencies. It is distinct from the routine operational stocks held by oil companies.

India's Phase I strategic crude-storage facilities, developed through Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited (ISPRL), have a combined storage capacity of 5.33 million metric tonnes. The completed facilities are:

Strategic reserve locationStateStorage capacity
VisakhapatnamAndhra Pradesh1.33 MMT
MangaloreKarnataka1.50 MMT
PadurKarnataka2.50 MMT

The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas identifies these 3 commissioned facilities as the completed Phase I storage network. It also records in-principle approval for an additional 4 MMT at Chandikhol, Odisha, and 2.5 MMT at Padur, Karnataka. These proposed additions must not be counted as already commissioned Phase I capacity.

Storage capacity is the maximum designed amount the facilities can hold; it is not necessarily the actual quantity of crude stored on a particular date. Reserve capacity expressed in tonnes also should not be described as a fixed number of days of national consumption without stating the consumption rate and assumptions used.

Strategic reserves improve resilience to interruptions, but they do not make India independent of imported oil. Supply diversification, domestic exploration, efficient fuel use and dependable transport infrastructure remain important.

Prelims focus

  • Brent and Dubai/Oman are important crude-oil price references.
  • Light and heavy describe crude density; sweet and sour describe sulphur characteristics.
  • OPEC and OPEC+ are not identical groupings.
  • India's commissioned Phase I strategic crude-storage capacity is 5.33 MMT.
  • Visakhapatnam is in Andhra Pradesh; Mangalore and Padur are in Karnataka.
  • Trap: In-principle approval for additional storage does not mean the new facility is commissioned.

[Sources: Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Strategic Crude Oil Storage, section on Phase I facilities and additional in-principle approvals, mopng.gov.in, page updated 6 October 2026; Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserve Limited, International Cooperation section; Indian Oil Corporation, Gujarat Refinery, Mode of Product Dispatch; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, chapter 7, section Petroleum; consulted 15 November 2026.]

body:
What natural gas contains

Natural gas is a naturally occurring gaseous mixture of hydrocarbons containing mainly methane. Its composition varies by deposit and may include other hydrocarbons and impurities that require removal before supply to consumers.

Natural gas may occur together with crude oil or in reservoirs that primarily contain gas. Associated gas is produced in association with oil. Non-associated gas comes from a reservoir containing gas without significant associated oil production. Both originate from geological processes involving organic material.

Processing and uses

Raw natural gas commonly undergoes treatment to remove water and undesirable substances before transportation. Depending on the gas composition and processing system, valuable heavier hydrocarbons may also be separated.

Natural gas is used as a fuel for industry, electricity generation and cooking. It is also a chemical feedstock. In the fertiliser industry, natural gas is an important raw material for producing hydrogen, which is used to manufacture ammonia and subsequently nitrogen fertilisers such as urea.

Natural gas generally produces less carbon dioxide per unit of heat released than coal when burned. However, it is still a fossil fuel. Its climate impact also depends on methane leakage during production, processing and transportation because methane is a powerful greenhouse gas.

PNG, CNG, LNG and LPG are different

TermMeaning and physical formTypical use
PNGPiped natural gas delivered through a distribution networkHouseholds, commerce and industry
CNGCompressed natural gas stored at high pressureVehicle fuel
LNGLiquefied natural gas obtained by strong coolingBulk storage and long-distance transportation
LPGLiquefied petroleum gas, mainly propane and butaneCooking and industrial fuel

PNG, CNG and LNG commonly refer to different methods of delivering or storing methane-rich natural gas. LPG is a different fuel mixture, mainly propane and butane, obtained from petroleum refining and natural-gas processing. LNG and LPG are not interchangeable names.

Why natural gas is liquefied

Natural gas occupies a large volume at ordinary temperature and pressure. For long-distance marine transportation, it is cooled to approximately −162 °C, causing methane-rich gas to become liquid. The liquid occupies far less volume than the original gas, making shipment in specially insulated tankers practical.

At an importing terminal, LNG is unloaded and stored in insulated facilities. It is then warmed in a regasification process to return it to gaseous form. The regasified natural gas enters the pipeline network or is supplied through other suitable distribution arrangements.

Natural-gas pipeline networks

High-pressure transmission pipelines move natural gas over long distances from producing regions or import terminals towards major consumption centres. Local distribution networks subsequently supply households, commercial users, vehicles and industries.

Gas pipelines differ from petroleum-product pipelines. A natural-gas transmission pipeline carries gaseous fuel, whereas a product pipeline may carry liquids such as petrol or diesel. LNG can also be transported in cryogenic road tankers to users not connected to the main transmission network.

India's natural-gas regions

Important Indian natural-gas-producing regions include the Mumbai offshore area, the Krishna-Godavari Basin, parts of Assam and Tripura, and gas-bearing regions of Gujarat and Rajasthan. The geographical distribution of gas fields influences pipeline routes and industrial development.

Gujarat's LNG infrastructure

Gujarat has several important LNG import-terminal locations, including Dahej, Hazira and Mundra. Their coastal locations permit LNG tankers to discharge imported gas, which can then be regasified and supplied to inland consumers.

Petronet LNG notified that the expansion of the Dahej LNG terminal from 17.5 million metric tonnes per annum to 22.5 million metric tonnes per annum was commissioned on 31 March 2026. The company formally disclosed this development on 1 April 2026. Capacity describes the terminal's annual processing capability, not the amount of LNG actually imported in a particular year.

The availability of LNG import infrastructure can increase the diversity of India's natural-gas supply. However, gas imported through an LNG terminal remains an imported energy source and exposes users to international gas prices and shipping conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Methane is the principal constituent of natural gas.
  • Associated gas occurs with oil; non-associated gas comes from predominantly gas-bearing reservoirs.
  • LNG is natural gas liquefied by cooling to approximately −162 °C.
  • LPG consists mainly of propane and butane; it is not the same as LNG.
  • Dahej, Hazira and Mundra are important LNG locations in Gujarat.
  • Trap: A larger LNG regasification capacity does not automatically imply greater actual LNG imports.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, chapter 5, Coal and Petroleum, section 5.3, Natural Gas, printed pp. 60–61; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, chapter 7, section Natural Gas, printed p. 80; Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Indian Petroleum and Natural Gas Statistics 2024–25, chapter III, table III.9, Status of LNG Terminals in India, printed p. 54; Petronet LNG Limited, stock-exchange disclosure on commissioning of additional Dahej LNG regasification facilities, 1 April 2026; consulted 15 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Methane-rich natural gas is cooled to LNG for insulated sea transport, unloaded and stored, then warmed back to gas for distribution; LNG differs from LPG.
pictures.caption: LNG is transported as a cryogenic liquid and returned to gas before pipeline distribution.

title: Natural Gas: Formation, Processing, LNG and Pipeline Supply

body:
What a city gas distribution network does

City Gas Distribution (CGD) is the system through which natural gas is supplied to consumers in an authorised geographical area. It commonly includes pipelines, pressure-regulating facilities, customer connections and CNG-filling stations.

The two most familiar products of a CGD network are piped natural gas (PNG) supplied to households, commercial premises or industries and compressed natural gas (CNG) supplied to vehicles. The underlying fuel is mainly methane-rich natural gas; the difference lies in the way it is supplied and used.

Role of the petroleum and natural-gas regulator

The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB) was established under the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Act, 2006. The Board has responsibilities relating to specified petroleum and natural-gas infrastructure, including the authorisation and regulation of city gas distribution networks and pipelines.

A geographical area (GA) is an area authorised for the development or operation of a CGD network. Authorising an area does not mean that every household within it is already connected. Network construction, consumer connections and gas sales are separate measures of actual service expansion.

Recent city-gas statistics

PNGRB's quarterly report for April–June 2026, dated 26 October 2026, recorded the following status as on 30 June 2026:

  • 309 authorised geographical areas across 34 states and union territories.
  • Approximately 1.74 crore domestic PNG connections.
  • 9,026 CNG stations.

These are dated infrastructure indicators, not estimates for November 2026. An authorised geographical area is not the same thing as an individual household connection or a CNG station.

Natural-gas pricing is not uniform

The price of natural gas depends on where it is produced, the applicable production and pricing rules, the terms of supply contracts and the costs of transportation and distribution.

Administered Price Mechanism (APM) gas refers to domestic natural gas supplied under a specified government pricing framework, particularly gas from eligible older nomination fields. Under the revised guidelines effective from 8 April 2023, the domestic APM gas price was linked to 10% of the Indian crude basket price, subject to the applicable floor and ceiling provisions for specified nomination-field gas. The price is notified monthly. For ONGC and Oil India nomination-field gas, the 2023 framework set a floor of US$4 and an initial ceiling of US$6.50 per million British thermal units, with annual US$0.25 ceiling increases from FY 2025–26.

Not all domestically produced gas follows the same APM conditions. Certain gas from deep-water, ultra-deep-water and high-pressure, high-temperature discoveries is subject to different pricing arrangements. Imported LNG may be priced under long-term contracts or linked to prevailing international market conditions.

The price paid by a PNG household or CNG vehicle owner also reflects transportation, distribution and other applicable charges. Consequently, the government-notified price for a category of domestic gas must not be treated as the final retail price paid by every consumer.

Domestic production, domestic APM pricing and retail CNG or PNG pricing are different concepts. A gas molecule may originate domestically or abroad, enter a transmission network, and finally be sold through a CGD operator under applicable supply and retail arrangements.

Gujarat's gas economy

Gujarat has a significant concentration of natural-gas infrastructure and consumers. Its coastal LNG terminals provide entry points for imported gas, while transmission and distribution networks connect industrial and urban demand centres.

The state has longstanding city-gas use, including an early piped-gas network in Vadodara. Industrial centres such as Ankleshwar, Dahej, Surat and Vapi are associated with natural-gas demand for manufacturing and other activities. Natural gas is useful in these industries as a controllable heat source or chemical feedstock.

Gujarat's LNG terminals, gas pipelines, refineries and oil-producing areas perform different functions. A refinery processes crude oil; an LNG terminal receives and regasifies imported natural gas; a pipeline transports fuel; and a CGD network delivers natural gas to final consumers.

How India can strengthen energy security

India's energy-security challenge arises from the interaction of several facts: coal remains important for primary energy and electricity, petroleum products are central to transport, and natural gas serves industry and households while relying partly on imports. These fuels cannot always be replaced directly by one another.

Measures for improving energy security include:

  • Domestic resources: responsible exploration and production of coal, oil and natural gas.
  • Import diversification: purchasing from multiple suppliers and maintaining alternative shipping and transport arrangements.
  • Strategic stocks: keeping emergency crude-oil reserves alongside normal commercial inventories.
  • Energy efficiency: reducing fuel required for a given amount of useful output.
  • Electricity transition: increasing suitable non-fossil generation, storage and network flexibility.
  • Demand-side measures: reducing wasteful consumption and using appropriate technologies for transport, buildings and industry.

These measures address different risks. More domestic coal can reduce some fuel-import exposure but does not eliminate combustion emissions. More LNG-import capacity can improve access to natural gas but does not remove dependence on international gas markets. More renewable electricity can reduce fossil-fuel use, but dependable supply still requires attention to generation patterns, electricity networks and storage.

The complete energy-system relationship

The central relationships are: coal is extracted and commonly used to generate electricity or provide industrial heat; crude oil is produced domestically or imported, refined and supplied mainly as petroleum products; and natural gas is produced or imported as LNG, processed and transported through pipelines for industry, fertilisers, cooking and vehicles.

India's completed Phase I strategic crude-oil storage capacity is 5.33 MMT, located at Visakhapatnam, Mangalore and Padur. This helps protect against petroleum-supply disruptions but does not replace the need for routine imports or efficient energy use. The resulting energy system must balance reliability, affordability, security and environmental protection.

Prelims focus

  • PNGRB was established under the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Act, 2006.
  • PNG means piped natural gas; CNG means compressed natural gas.
  • PNGRB recorded 309 authorised CGD geographical areas and 9,026 CNG stations as on 30 June 2026.
  • APM gas pricing and retail PNG or CNG prices are not identical.
  • Gujarat has important petroleum-refining, LNG-import and city-gas infrastructure.
  • Trap: A CGD geographical area being authorised does not mean every consumer in that area has a gas connection.

[Sources: Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board, Quarterly Progress Report on City Gas Distribution, Q1 FY 2026–27, preface and sector statistics, data as on 30 June 2026, report dated 26 October 2026; Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Act, 2006, and PNGRB CGD Authorisation Regulations, 2008, as amended; Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Indian Petroleum and Natural Gas Statistics 2024–25, section on Domestic Natural Gas Pricing Guidelines and their revision effective 8 April 2023; NCERT, Science, Class 8, chapter 5, section 5.3, Natural Gas, printed p. 61; Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Strategic Crude Oil Storage, Phase I facilities; consulted 15 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: India's energy security depends on the complete path from resources to final use.
